top_news.title: Drinking Water and Sanitation Department organises virtual conference as follow up to Water Summit
top_news.summary: The Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation (DDWS), Ministry of Jal Shakti, on Thursday organised the fourth virtual conference with States and Union Territories as part of a series of thematic consultations being held in follow-up to the Departmental Summit on Water 2026 held on 1-2 September. The conference focused on strengthening convergence between Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) 2.0 and the 16th Finance Commission to advance source sustainability, water security and Gram Panchayat-led planning for sustainable rural drinking water service delivery. The virtual conference brought together senior officials from State PHEDs/Rural Water Supply Departments, Panchayati Raj Departments and representatives from the Ministries of Panchayati Raj, Ministry of Rural Development, Government of India and National Informatics Centre. State rural water supply departments, including Karnataka, Odisha and Madhya Pradesh, shared best practices and field experiences on leveraging Finance Commission grants for strengthening rural water supply systems, improving O&M arrangements, enhancing community participation and strengthening local governance mechanisms. Addressing the conference, Ashok K.K. Meena, Secretary, DDWS, stated that with the extension of JJM 2.0, the focus now shifts from infrastructure creation to ensuring functionality, sustainability and quality service delivery. He emphasised that the true measure of success lies not merely in asset creation but in ensuring that rural households continue to receive reliable and safe drinking water through well-maintained and financially sustainable systems. Meena underlined the pivotal role of Gram Panchayats in rural water governance and noted that the 73rd Constitutional Amendment places drinking water and sanitation among the key responsibilities of local self-governments. He stressed that Gram Panchayats must take leadership in preparing comprehensive annual O&M plans, mobilising local resources, managing service delivery and ensuring accountability for water supply infrastructure created under JJM and other programmes. Referring to the 16th Finance Commission framework, he highlighted that tied grants provide a significant opportunity to strengthen the sustainability of drinking water and sanitation services at the grassroots level. He noted that of the total Rural Local Body (RLB) grants recommended by the 16th Finance Commission, a substantial share has been earmarked for water and sanitation-related activities. He emphasised that these grants should be utilised primarily for operation and maintenance, source sustainability, water quality management, service delivery improvements and strengthening local institutional capacity rather than creation of new infrastructure where existing assets require maintenance and support. The Secretary focused on three key pillars of sustainable financing for rural water supply systems such as effective utilisation of Finance Commission grants, ii. convergence with other available programmes, and iii. schemes, and progressive strengthening of user-charge collection mechanisms. Referring to successful examples from several States, he encouraged States and Gram Panchayats to adopt sustainable revenue models that support recurring O&M expenditure and reduce dependence on a single funding source. He also stressed the growing role of Gram Panchayats in the management of sanitation and solid waste systems and highlighted the need for local bodies to plan comprehensively for both drinking water and sanitation services. He noted that adequate provisions must be made for repairs, leak management, pump maintenance, chlorination, water-quality surveillance, electricity expenditure and staffing arrangements required for uninterrupted service delivery. Emphasising capacity building as a critical requirement, Meena called upon States to utilise resources available under the Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan (RGSA) and other programmes for training Panchayat representatives and local functionaries. He urged States to translate and disseminate Operation and Maintenance Manuals in local languages and ensure that Panchayats clearly understand the permissible activities, funding mechanisms and reporting requirements under the Finance Commission framework. He called upon to strengthen coordination between Rural Water Supply Departments, Panchayati Raj Institutions and Rural Development Departments at the State, district and Gram Panchayat levels. He noted that the simultaneous implementation of JJM 2.0, VB-G RAM G, and the 16th Finance Commission cycle provides a unique opportunity to institutionalise sustainable water governance through integrated planning and coordinated implementation. Kritika Kulhari, Deputy Secretary, NJJM, made a detailed presentation on the 16th Finance Commission Grants and utilisation of tied grants for water and sanitation, outlining the grant structure, release conditions, reporting requirements, permissible activities and planning framework. Participants were informed that the total Rural Local Body allocation under the 16th Finance Commission exceeds 4.35 lakh crore, with nearly 1.74 lakh crore earmarked for water management and sanitation over the award period. The presentation highlighted that priority should be accorded to operation and maintenance of existing assets, lifecycle-based planning, preventive maintenance, community ownership and digital accountability through prescribed platforms. Vipul Ujwal, Director, Ministry of Panchayati Raj, made a detailed presentation on GPDP planning, release modalities and utilisation of Finance Commission Grants for rural water supply O&M. He emphasised that sustainable service delivery requires integration of three critical elements - Requirements, Resources and Responsibilities (RRR). He explained how Gram Panchayats should identify service gaps, estimate annual O&M requirements, assess available financial resources and integrate these priorities into the Gram Panchayat Development Plan (GPDP). He further highlighted the growing importance of Own Source Revenue (OSR), user-charge collection and performance-based grants in strengthening Panchayat finances and ensuring sustainable service delivery. The conference also featured a technical presentation by NIC, Ministry of Panchayati Raj, on the eGramSwaraj portal and its reporting modules. The session explained how Gram Panchayats can integrate planning, implementation, geo-tagging, expenditure reporting, asset management and monitoring through the digital platform. The presentation highlighted the integration of eGramSwaraj with the Public Financial Management System (PFMS) and various departmental databases, enabling improved transparency, accountability and real-time monitoring of Finance Commission-funded activities. During the State experience-sharing session, Karnataka presented its integrated approach to rural water supply management through innovations such as Jala Sankalana, JalaAasthi and Jeevajala, which combine GIS-based asset management, real-time monitoring, community participation and evidence-based O&M planning. The State highlighted its experience in water budgeting, volumetric tariff collection, preventive maintenance and strengthening community ownership of drinking water systems. Further, the state shared its experience of institutional convergence under the Rural Development and Panchayat Raj framework, where Rural Water Supply, Panchayati Raj and Rural Development functions operate in close coordination and highlighted how this integrated administrative structure has enabled better planning and utilisation of Finance Commission grants, strengthened Gram Panchayat participation in operation and maintenance planning, water budgeting and tariff collection, and improved coordination between technical departments and local self-governments. Karnataka emphasised that sustained community engagement, clear delineation of responsibilities and convergence of financial resources have been central to strengthening the long-term sustainability of rural drinking water services. Odisha shared its institutional model built around close convergence among Rural Development, Panchayati Raj and Drinking Water departments. The State presented its integrated O&M framework, bottom-up budgeting process, digital monitoring systems, local mechanic training programmes and technology-driven interventions such as solarisation, automation and IoT-based monitoring systems aimed at ensuring long-term sustainability of drinking water services. The State highlighted how coordinated planning, bottom-up budgeting and convergence of Finance Commission grants, State resources and community contributions have helped strengthen operation and maintenance systems. Odisha also underscored the importance of Gram Panchayat participation, local capacity building, digital monitoring and clearly defined accountability mechanisms in ensuring reliable service delivery and sustainable management of rural water supply infrastructure. Madhya Pradesh highlighted its recently notified O&M Rules, 2026, which enable Gram Panchayats to utilise multiple funding streams for water supply and sanitation activities. The State showcased simplified procurement processes, district-level WASH technical committees, structured training programmes, digital systems for user-charge collection and extensive efforts to build technical capacity among Panchayat representatives and engineers. The State highlighted how multiple funding streams, including Finance Commission grants, State grants, user charges and other local resources, are being brought together to support sustainable operation and maintenance. In his concluding remarks, Kamal Kishore Soan, AS&MD, NJJM reiterated that Finance Commission grants should be viewed as an opportunity to institutionalise sustainable rural water governance and strengthen Panchayat ownership of water supply systems. He urged States to complete pending compliance requirements, strengthen GPDP-based planning, improve user-charge collection mechanisms, and ensure effective utilisation of both 15th and 16th Finance Commission grants for sustaining rural water supply infrastructure. Soan also called upon States to organise intensive training and capacity-building programmes for Panchayat representatives, Panchayat Secretaries, Sarpanches and technical personnel over the coming months and ensure timely resolution of eGramSwaraj login and reporting issues. He informed participants that two regional conferences are planned in November 2026 to review preparedness, address implementation challenges and strengthen convergence among departments responsible for drinking water, sanitation, Panchayati Raj and Rural Development. The conference concluded with a shared commitment by the Centre and States/UTs to strengthen Panchayat-led planning, improve financial sustainability, enhance interdepartmental convergence and ensure that the substantial investments made under Jal Jeevan Mission translate into reliable, continuous and sustainable drinking water and sanitation services for rural households across the country. (ANI)

top_news.title: Mehdi Hasan on AIPAC’s Role in El-Sayed vs. Rogers Race in Michigan & Trump’s Targeting of Ilhan Omar
top_news.summary: One of the most closely watched races in the midterm elections is in Michigan between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers. El-Sayed is a former public health official who is campaigning on a platform of Medicare for All, ending military aid to Israel, and getting corporate money out of politics. Rogers is a former Republican congressman backed by President Trump. If elected, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim to serve in the U.S. Senate. During Wednesday’s debate in Michigan, Rogers repeated the claim, without providing evidence, that El-Sayed has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed has repeatedly denied the accusation. “If Abdul El-Sayed wins, it will be a reminder that the left can win in a swing state like Michigan,” says Mehdi Hasan, editor-in-chief of Zeteo. “And it will be actually a moment to say, 'You know what? Americans rejected Islamophobia.'”

Soon after he was appointed the country's home minister, he took decisive historical decisions to enhance India's national security during the tenure of the Modi 2.0 govt in 2019. Born to Kusumben and Anilchandra Shah in an affluent Gujarati family on October 22, 1964, Shah has been remarkably successful in expanding the Bharatiya Janata Party's organisational footprint by leading the party from the front and securing one electoral victory after the other in state assembly elections. During his tenure as BJP President, the BJP became the world's largest political party with over 10 crore registered members. Shah, who joined the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh and later became an active member of the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) during his youth, has risen to head the ruling Party of India literally from the grassroots. His dedication, dexterity and above all result-oriented performance made Shah in-charge of several election campaigns of the national leaders, including that of LK Advani in 1991, late Atal Bihari Vajpayee in 1996, both in the Gandhinagar Parliamentary constituency in Gujarat. In 2013, Shah was appointed as National General Secretary of the BJP and in-charge of Uttar Pradesh. His painstakingly carried out efforts earned the BJP a historic success in the Parliamentary elections of 2014. He took over as BJP National President in July 2014, and from there onwards there is literally no looking back. By May 2018, in the direction of Shah, the BJP and its alliance partners were in government in 21 states, reflecting the scale of the party's electoral expansion Shah, who assumed charge as Union Home Minister in the Modi 2.0 government on June 1, 2019, took one of the most consequential and historical decisions within two months in office. It was the abrogation of Article 370, which had granted special status to the erstwhile state of Jammu and Kashmir. Later, in August 2019, the government moved to end the region's special constitutional status and reorganised the state into the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh. The move represented a major departure in the Centre's approach to Jammu and Kashmir and became one of the defining policy decisions of Shah's tenure. The government maintained that the changes would facilitate integration, development and improved security in the region. The decision also generated substantial political and legal debate, making it one of the most significant constitutional developments of the period. Shah's tenure has also been marked by major legislative changes like the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019, which was passed by Parliament during the first year of his tenure. The legislation provides an expedited route to Indian citizenship for eligible Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi and Christian migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who entered India by December 31, 2014, subject to the Act's conditions and applicable exclusions. articles.title: Drinking Water and Sanitation Department organises virtual conference as follow up to Water Summit
articles.summary: The Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation (DDWS), Ministry of Jal Shakti, on Thursday organised the fourth virtual conference with States and Union Territories as part of a series of thematic consultations being held in follow-up to the Departmental Summit on Water 2026 held on 1-2 September. The conference focused on strengthening convergence between Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) 2.0 and the 16th Finance Commission to advance source sustainability, water security and Gram Panchayat-led planning for sustainable rural drinking water service delivery. The virtual conference brought together senior officials from State PHEDs/Rural Water Supply Departments, Panchayati Raj Departments and representatives from the Ministries of Panchayati Raj, Ministry of Rural Development, Government of India and National Informatics Centre. State rural water supply departments, including Karnataka, Odisha and Madhya Pradesh, shared best practices and field experiences on leveraging Finance Commission grants for strengthening rural water supply systems, improving O&M arrangements, enhancing community participation and strengthening local governance mechanisms. Addressing the conference, Ashok K.K. Meena, Secretary, DDWS, stated that with the extension of JJM 2.0, the focus now shifts from infrastructure creation to ensuring functionality, sustainability and quality service delivery. He emphasised that the true measure of success lies not merely in asset creation but in ensuring that rural households continue to receive reliable and safe drinking water through well-maintained and financially sustainable systems. Meena underlined the pivotal role of Gram Panchayats in rural water governance and noted that the 73rd Constitutional Amendment places drinking water and sanitation among the key responsibilities of local self-governments. He stressed that Gram Panchayats must take leadership in preparing comprehensive annual O&M plans, mobilising local resources, managing service delivery and ensuring accountability for water supply infrastructure created under JJM and other programmes. Referring to the 16th Finance Commission framework, he highlighted that tied grants provide a significant opportunity to strengthen the sustainability of drinking water and sanitation services at the grassroots level. He noted that of the total Rural Local Body (RLB) grants recommended by the 16th Finance Commission, a substantial share has been earmarked for water and sanitation-related activities. He emphasised that these grants should be utilised primarily for operation and maintenance, source sustainability, water quality management, service delivery improvements and strengthening local institutional capacity rather than creation of new infrastructure where existing assets require maintenance and support. The Secretary focused on three key pillars of sustainable financing for rural water supply systems such as effective utilisation of Finance Commission grants, ii. convergence with other available programmes, and iii. schemes, and progressive strengthening of user-charge collection mechanisms. Referring to successful examples from several States, he encouraged States and Gram Panchayats to adopt sustainable revenue models that support recurring O&M expenditure and reduce dependence on a single funding source. He also stressed the growing role of Gram Panchayats in the management of sanitation and solid waste systems and highlighted the need for local bodies to plan comprehensively for both drinking water and sanitation services. He noted that adequate provisions must be made for repairs, leak management, pump maintenance, chlorination, water-quality surveillance, electricity expenditure and staffing arrangements required for uninterrupted service delivery. Emphasising capacity building as a critical requirement, Meena called upon States to utilise resources available under the Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan (RGSA) and other programmes for training Panchayat representatives and local functionaries. He urged States to translate and disseminate Operation and Maintenance Manuals in local languages and ensure that Panchayats clearly understand the permissible activities, funding mechanisms and reporting requirements under the Finance Commission framework. He called upon to strengthen coordination between Rural Water Supply Departments, Panchayati Raj Institutions and Rural Development Departments at the State, district and Gram Panchayat levels. He noted that the simultaneous implementation of JJM 2.0, VB-G RAM G, and the 16th Finance Commission cycle provides a unique opportunity to institutionalise sustainable water governance through integrated planning and coordinated implementation. Kritika Kulhari, Deputy Secretary, NJJM, made a detailed presentation on the 16th Finance Commission Grants and utilisation of tied grants for water and sanitation, outlining the grant structure, release conditions, reporting requirements, permissible activities and planning framework. Participants were informed that the total Rural Local Body allocation under the 16th Finance Commission exceeds 4.35 lakh crore, with nearly 1.74 lakh crore earmarked for water management and sanitation over the award period. The presentation highlighted that priority should be accorded to operation and maintenance of existing assets, lifecycle-based planning, preventive maintenance, community ownership and digital accountability through prescribed platforms. Vipul Ujwal, Director, Ministry of Panchayati Raj, made a detailed presentation on GPDP planning, release modalities and utilisation of Finance Commission Grants for rural water supply O&M. He emphasised that sustainable service delivery requires integration of three critical elements - Requirements, Resources and Responsibilities (RRR). He explained how Gram Panchayats should identify service gaps, estimate annual O&M requirements, assess available financial resources and integrate these priorities into the Gram Panchayat Development Plan (GPDP). He further highlighted the growing importance of Own Source Revenue (OSR), user-charge collection and performance-based grants in strengthening Panchayat finances and ensuring sustainable service delivery. The conference also featured a technical presentation by NIC, Ministry of Panchayati Raj, on the eGramSwaraj portal and its reporting modules. The session explained how Gram Panchayats can integrate planning, implementation, geo-tagging, expenditure reporting, asset management and monitoring through the digital platform. The presentation highlighted the integration of eGramSwaraj with the Public Financial Management System (PFMS) and various departmental databases, enabling improved transparency, accountability and real-time monitoring of Finance Commission-funded activities. During the State experience-sharing session, Karnataka presented its integrated approach to rural water supply management through innovations such as Jala Sankalana, JalaAasthi and Jeevajala, which combine GIS-based asset management, real-time monitoring, community participation and evidence-based O&M planning. The State highlighted its experience in water budgeting, volumetric tariff collection, preventive maintenance and strengthening community ownership of drinking water systems. Further, the state shared its experience of institutional convergence under the Rural Development and Panchayat Raj framework, where Rural Water Supply, Panchayati Raj and Rural Development functions operate in close coordination and highlighted how this integrated administrative structure has enabled better planning and utilisation of Finance Commission grants, strengthened Gram Panchayat participation in operation and maintenance planning, water budgeting and tariff collection, and improved coordination between technical departments and local self-governments. Karnataka emphasised that sustained community engagement, clear delineation of responsibilities and convergence of financial resources have been central to strengthening the long-term sustainability of rural drinking water services. Odisha shared its institutional model built around close convergence among Rural Development, Panchayati Raj and Drinking Water departments. The State presented its integrated O&M framework, bottom-up budgeting process, digital monitoring systems, local mechanic training programmes and technology-driven interventions such as solarisation, automation and IoT-based monitoring systems aimed at ensuring long-term sustainability of drinking water services. The State highlighted how coordinated planning, bottom-up budgeting and convergence of Finance Commission grants, State resources and community contributions have helped strengthen operation and maintenance systems. Odisha also underscored the importance of Gram Panchayat participation, local capacity building, digital monitoring and clearly defined accountability mechanisms in ensuring reliable service delivery and sustainable management of rural water supply infrastructure. Madhya Pradesh highlighted its recently notified O&M Rules, 2026, which enable Gram Panchayats to utilise multiple funding streams for water supply and sanitation activities. The State showcased simplified procurement processes, district-level WASH technical committees, structured training programmes, digital systems for user-charge collection and extensive efforts to build technical capacity among Panchayat representatives and engineers. The State highlighted how multiple funding streams, including Finance Commission grants, State grants, user charges and other local resources, are being brought together to support sustainable operation and maintenance. In his concluding remarks, Kamal Kishore Soan, AS&MD, NJJM reiterated that Finance Commission grants should be viewed as an opportunity to institutionalise sustainable rural water governance and strengthen Panchayat ownership of water supply systems. He urged States to complete pending compliance requirements, strengthen GPDP-based planning, improve user-charge collection mechanisms, and ensure effective utilisation of both 15th and 16th Finance Commission grants for sustaining rural water supply infrastructure. Soan also called upon States to organise intensive training and capacity-building programmes for Panchayat representatives, Panchayat Secretaries, Sarpanches and technical personnel over the coming months and ensure timely resolution of eGramSwaraj login and reporting issues. He informed participants that two regional conferences are planned in November 2026 to review preparedness, address implementation challenges and strengthen convergence among departments responsible for drinking water, sanitation, Panchayati Raj and Rural Development. The conference concluded with a shared commitment by the Centre and States/UTs to strengthen Panchayat-led planning, improve financial sustainability, enhance interdepartmental convergence and ensure that the substantial investments made under Jal Jeevan Mission translate into reliable, continuous and sustainable drinking water and sanitation services for rural households across the country. (ANI)

articles.title: Mehdi Hasan on AIPAC’s Role in El-Sayed vs. Rogers Race in Michigan & Trump’s Targeting of Ilhan Omar
articles.summary: One of the most closely watched races in the midterm elections is in Michigan between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers. El-Sayed is a former public health official who is campaigning on a platform of Medicare for All, ending military aid to Israel, and getting corporate money out of politics. Rogers is a former Republican congressman backed by President Trump. If elected, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim to serve in the U.S. Senate. During Wednesday’s debate in Michigan, Rogers repeated the claim, without providing evidence, that El-Sayed has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed has repeatedly denied the accusation. “If Abdul El-Sayed wins, it will be a reminder that the left can win in a swing state like Michigan,” says Mehdi Hasan, editor-in-chief of Zeteo. “And it will be actually a moment to say, 'You know what? Americans rejected Islamophobia.'”

articles.title: From BJP
articles.summary: Known in bureaucratic and political circles as a "man of commitment", Union Home Minister Amit Shah, who turns 62 on October 22, has emerged as one of the most influential figures in Indian politics in his past 12-year career by expanding the BJP's political footprint across India since taking over the party's command as its President in 2014. Soon after he was appointed the country's home minister, he took decisive historical decisions to enhance India's national security during the tenure of the Modi 2.0 govt in 2019. Born to Kusumben and Anilchandra Shah in an affluent Gujarati family on October 22, 1964, Shah has been remarkably successful in expanding the Bharatiya Janata Party's organisational footprint by leading the party from the front and securing one electoral victory after the other in state assembly elections. During his tenure as BJP President, the BJP became the world's largest political party with over 10 crore registered members. Shah, who joined the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh and later became an active member of the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) during his youth, has risen to head the ruling Party of India literally from the grassroots. His dedication, dexterity and above all result-oriented performance made Shah in-charge of several election campaigns of the national leaders, including that of LK Advani in 1991, late Atal Bihari Vajpayee in 1996, both in the Gandhinagar Parliamentary constituency in Gujarat. In 2013, Shah was appointed as National General Secretary of the BJP and in-charge of Uttar Pradesh. His painstakingly carried out efforts earned the BJP a historic success in the Parliamentary elections of 2014. He took over as BJP National President in July 2014, and from there onwards there is literally no looking back. By May 2018, in the direction of Shah, the BJP and its alliance partners were in government in 21 states, reflecting the scale of the party's electoral expansion Shah, who assumed charge as Union Home Minister in the Modi 2.0 government on June 1, 2019, took one of the most consequential and historical decisions within two months in office. It was the abrogation of Article 370, which had granted special status to the erstwhile state of Jammu and Kashmir. Later, in August 2019, the government moved to end the region's special constitutional status and reorganised the state into the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh. The move represented a major departure in the Centre's approach to Jammu and Kashmir and became one of the defining policy decisions of Shah's tenure. The government maintained that the changes would facilitate integration, development and improved security in the region. The decision also generated substantial political and legal debate, making it one of the most significant constitutional developments of the period. Shah's tenure has also been marked by major legislative changes like the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019, which was passed by Parliament during the first year of his tenure. The legislation provides an expedited route to Indian citizenship for eligible Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi and Christian migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who entered India by December 31, 2014, subject to the Act's conditions and applicable exclusions. articles.title: Voters prioritize costs and Iran over investigating Trump for next Congress, AP-NORC poll finds
articles.summary: A new AP-NORC poll shows voters from both major political parties want the next Congress to focus on making life more affordable and ending the war in Iran. Fewer are looking for an emphasis on President Donald Trump — whether it’s investigating him or supporting his Republican agenda. The results suggest that voters of both parties are ready for Congress to tackle core issues, despite Trump’s centrality in the midterm campaign. About 8 in 10 registered voters, including most Republicans and Democrats, say lowering the cost of living should be one of the highest priorities for the coming session.
